name: Register Switching Drill - Patient, Team, Attending
_note: Skill drill focused on changing the same clinical meaning across patient-friendly language, team communication, and attending-style summaries. This is an English register drill, not a diagnostic simulation.

anchors.90-100: Clear, controlled sentences in all registers
anchors.50-60: Understandable but with repeated sentence problems
anchors.30-40: Frequent errors make register switching hard to follow

anchors.90-100: Preserves the clinical meaning accurately while changing register
anchors.70-80: Mostly preserves meaning with minor imprecision
anchors.50-60: Gets the gist but drops or changes some important details
anchors.30-40: Several facts are distorted or invented
anchors.10-20: Meaning is often wrong or unsafe

anchors.90-100: Patient version is plain, team version concise, attending version structured
anchors.50-60: Some mismatch, such as jargon with patients or vague team updates
anchors.30-40: Often uses the wrong register for the listener
anchors.10-20: Cannot shift language for different listeners

anchors.90-100: Switches smoothly between versions with natural pace
Tone fits each listener: respectful, clear, and confident
anchors.50-60: Acceptable but sometimes too casual or too technical
anchors.30-40: Tone is often mismatched or unclear
anchors.10-20: Tone would undermine trust or teamwork

checklist.item: created a patient-friendly version using plain everyday words
created a concise team update for a nurse or colleague
created a structured attending-style summary or recommendation
preserved the original clinical meaning without inventing facts
used signposting such as 'In simple terms', 'My concern is', or 'I recommend'
asked for clarification when the prompt was unclear
